data.title: Pengaruh Gambler’s Fallacy dan Illusion of Control terhadap Keputusan Investasi Investor Ritel

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.63643/fbr.v6i1.339?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.63643/fbr.v6i1.339, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis pengaruh Gambler’s Fallacy dan Illusion of Control terhadap keputusan investasi investor ritel dalam perspektif behavioral finance. Penelitian ini mengguankan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan data primer yang diperoleh melalui penyebaran kuesioner kepada 100 investor ritel di Kota Batam. Teknik analisis data yang digunakan adalah Structural Equation Modeling berbasis Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) dengan bantuan aplikasi SmartPLS. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa Gambler’s Fallacy dan Illusion of Control berpengaruh positif dan signifikan terhadap keputusan investasi, baik secara parsial maupun simultan. Nilai R-Square sebesar 0,574 mengindikasikan bahwa kedua variabel mampu menjelaskan 57,4% variasi keputusan investasi, sedangkan sisanya dipengaruhi oleh faktor lain di luar model penelitian. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa keputusan investasi investor tidak sepenuhnya rasional, melainkan dipengaruhi oleh bias psikologis. Oleh karena itu, pemahaman terhadap bias kognitif menjadi penting dalam meningkatkan kualitas pengambilan keputusan investasi

data.title: Illusion of Control, Gambler's Fallacy, or Neither? Testing Key Models of Gambling Psychology by Extending Langer and Roth (1975).

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1007/s10899-026-10575-3?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1007/s10899-026-10575-3, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Cognitive biases about randomness, such as the illusion of control and the gambler's fallacy, are central to the widely-used cognitive models of disordered gambling. In a highly-cited foundational paper, Langer and Roth (1975) found that participants thought they were better at predicting coin-flips when they were randomised to receive more wins at the start rather than the end of a 30-flip sequence. This replicable effect, which has been attributed to the illusion of control, could also be driven by biases that do not involve active involvement, such as the gambler's fallacy. We therefore designed a large-scale (N = 1,594) online 2 × 2 experiment, where the sequence manipulation was crossed with a manipulation of active involvement. In the "self" condition, participants predicted and performed the coin-flips personally, whereas in the "other" condition, participants observed another participant predicting and performing the flips. The original effect of sequence replicated, occurring across both "self" and "other" conditions. However, participants in the "other" condition consistently rated the participants they observed as being better at predicting coin-flips than participants in the "self" condition rated their own abilities, an effect consistent with neither the illusion of control nor the gambler's fallacy. Furthermore, participants' Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) scores did not correlate with their ratings of coin-flip predictions. We conclude that while Langer and Roth's sequence effect is replicable, it is not attributable to the illusion of control or the gambler's fallacy, and may be a poor analogue of chance-based naturalistic gambling formats due to its lack of association with PGSI scores.

data.title: The Illusion of Rationality: Tacit Bias and Strategic Dominance in Frontier LLM Negotiation Games

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09254, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed as autonomous agents on behalf of institutions and individuals in economic, political, and social settings that involve negotiation. Yet, this trend carries significant risks if their strategic behavior is not well understood. In this work, we revisit the NegotiationArena framework and run controlled simulation experiments on a diverse set of frontier LLMs across three multiturn bargaining games: buyer–seller, multiturn ultimatum, and resource exchange. We ask whether improved general reasoning capabilities lead to rational, unbiased, and convergent negotiation strategies. Our results challenge this assumption. We find that models diverge into distinct, model-specific strategic equilibria rather than converging to a unified optimal behavior. Moreover, strong numerical and semantic anchoring effects persist: initial offers are highly predictive of final agreements, and models consistently generate biased proposals by collapsing diverse internal valuations into rigid, generic price points. Additionally, concerningly, we observe dominance patterns, in which some models systematically achieve higher payoffs than their counterparts. These findings underscore a clear need to develop mechanisms to mitigate these issues before deploying such systems in real-world scenarios.

data.title: Label Over Logic? How Source Cues Bias Human Fallacy Judgments More Than LLMs

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29928, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: As AI-generated and AI-assisted content floods online spaces, source labels attached to such content can distort human reasoning judgments, with downstream consequences for moderation, evaluation, and decision-making. Whether LLMs share this vulnerability, or offer more source-agnostic evaluation, remains an open question with strong implications for human-AI collaboration. We examine this issue using logical fallacies as a controlled setting to isolate source-label effects on reasoning quality, independent of domain knowledge. We conduct an online study (N=505) where participants are assigned to a source condition (human, AI, human with AI assistance, AI with human assistance, or no disclosure) and evaluate comments containing logical fallacies, comparing their judgments with those of LLMs (GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5), which were evaluated across the same source conditions. Human evaluators were significantly more susceptible to fallacies labeled as'written by human'or'written by human with AI assistance'and assigned higher trust ratings in these conditions. LLM evaluations remained comparatively stable across source labels, though performance varied across models. Confidence levels were similarly high across conditions for both humans and LLMs, regardless of the presence of fallacies. Our findings indicate that source-label bias is primarily a human vulnerability for logical fallacy evaluation, with potential implications in human-LLM collaboration in increasingly AI-mediated environments.

data.title: THE GENDER BIAS IN THE FALLACY OF APATHY AND MYTH OF IMPARTIAL LAW

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.61955/sfzjne?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.61955/sfzjne, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Traditional legal theory often claims that the law is neutral and fair, equating justice with the absence of emotion. This supposed impartiality hides biases and allows social inequalities to continue under the guise of objectivity. Gender, race, and class are frequently ignored in legal reasoning, which perpetuates rather than corrects injustice. This paper critiques legal indifference, showing how the law‟s appearance of neutrality sustains inequality. It argues for a legal approach that considers human experience as central to achieving real equality. Using a critical theoretical method, the study focuses on gender as a disadvantaged group. Legal doctrines, case law, and scholarly writings are analyzed to show how dispassionate reasoning masks power relations and structural disparities. Findings indicate that legal indifference does not remove bias; it hides it, turning equality into a formal promise rather than reality. Emotional detachment in law reinforces existing hierarchies and harms marginalized groups. The paper concludes that the idea of impartial law is a fallacy. To achieve substantive equality, legal reasoning must recognize lived experience and social context. A critical, empathetic perspective can break the illusion of neutrality and support fairer outcomes for all.

data.title: The Illusion of Procedural Reasoning: Measuring Long-Horizon FSM Execution in LLMs

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14777, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable results on tasks framed as reasoning problems, yet their true ability to perform procedural reasoning, executing multi-step, rule-based computations remains unclear. Unlike algorithmic systems, which can deterministically execute long-horizon symbolic procedures, LLMs often degrade under extended reasoning chains, but there is no controlled, interpretable benchmark to isolate and measure this collapse. We introduce Finite-State Machine (FSM) Execution as a minimal, fully interpretable framework for evaluating the procedural reasoning capacity of LLMs. In our setup, the model is given an explicit FSM definition and must execute it step-by-step given input actions, maintaining state consistency over multiple turns. This task requires no world knowledge, only faithful application of deterministic transition rules, making it a direct probe of the model's internal procedural fidelity. We measure both Turn Accuracy and Task Accuracy to disentangle immediate computation from cumulative state maintenance. Empirical results reveal systematic degradation as task horizon or branching complexity increases. Models perform significantly worse when rule retrieval involves high branching factors than when memory span is long. Larger models show improved local accuracy but remain brittle under multi-step reasoning unless explicitly prompted to externalize intermediate steps. FSM-based evaluation offers a transparent, complexity-controlled probe for diagnosing this failure mode and guiding the design of inductive biases that enable genuine long-horizon procedural competence. By grounding reasoning in measurable execution fidelity rather than surface correctness, this work helps establish a rigorous experimental foundation for understanding and improving the algorithmic reliability of LLMs.

data.abstract: In recent years, and especially during the on-going pandemic, the interest in investigating the dynamics of infodemics has increased to unprecedented levels. In this study we propose an agent-based model for the spread of misinformation, disinformation, and other similar information. The model is based on the susceptible-infected-recovered-susceptible epidemic interpretation. We introduce a rule-based reasoning module to model individual bias in the perception of information based on the psychology concept of illusion of knowledge. We integrate this module into a deliberative-reactive agent controller structure and a decentralized control scheme for the multi-agent system. Results show significant differences between the outputs of the proposed model and the classical version, impressing on the effects of considering local agent individuality when modeling human psycho-social interactions.

data.title: Automation's Not Perfect But Neither Are We: Unveiling Illusionary Control And Automation Bias In Automated Driving

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1145/3581961.3609897?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1145/3581961.3609897, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: If we want to develop automated vehicles that are truly human-centered, we need to keep in mind that our reasoning ability is far from “flawless”, as we are susceptible to inherent cognitive biases. With this work, we aim to systemically investigate cognitive biases in the context of automated driving for the first time. Using an online study (N = 99) and a short experiment (N = 21), we investigated two exemplary cognitive biases (1. illusion of control and 2. automation bias). Our results suggest that both can occur during automated driving. Specifically, we found that not only a greater amount of information about vehicle behavior but also the humanization of this information can lead to an (illusory) higher sense of control.

data.title: Simulated souls: investigating the emotional fallacy in large language models

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.2139/ssrn.5404666?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5404666, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence has ushered in a new era where machines produce text with such emotional coherence that they blur the boundary between simulation and sentience. This paper explores the emotional fallacy —a cognitive bias wherein users and even developers anthropomorphize Large Language Models (LLMs), attributing genuine emotions to systems governed solely by statistical inference and pattern recognition. While LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Meta AI are engineered to generate emotionally evocative content, their responses are frequently mistaken as indicators of self-awareness, affective reasoning, or internal states. This anthropomorphic illusion carries significant implications for user trust, emotional labour, and the broader ethical landscape of AI deployment. Through a novel empirical study, we evaluate the responses of multiple LLMs to a curated set of emotionally charged and ethically sensitive prompts. The outputs are analyzed qualitatively across three dimensions: linguistic style, affective mimicry, and ethical stance. Our findings reveal a paradox: while LLMs simulate emotion with impressive linguistic precision, they lack any true experiential grounding—underscoring their inherent emotional inauthenticity. To address these concerns, we propose an ethical framework that includes affective transparency, disclosure protocols, and regulation to prevent emotional manipulation in public-facing AI systems. We argue that the unchecked spread of the emotional fallacy may distort public perceptions of AI, affect mental health, and reshape norms surrounding machine consciousness and empathy. By integrating philosophical inquiry, empirical analysis, and ethical design, this paper calls for a paradigm shift—from emotional realism to emotional accountability in the design and deployment of generative AI. Our work offers a cautionary lens and a research frontier in the study of human–AI emotional interaction, particularly as such systems permeate education, healthcare, and psychological support domains.

data.title: Thinking fast and biased: intuitive thinking style is associated with the illusion of causality.

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1016/j.concog.2026.104045?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2026.104045, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The illusion of causality is a cognitive bias in which individuals believe that a potential cause produces an outcome even when the contingency between the two is null. Although no definitive theoretical explanation has been established for this bias, it has been linked to heuristic or associative processes that operate automatically and rely on intuition rather than deliberate reasoning. In this paper, we present two pre-registered studies examining the relationship between intuitive-deliberate thinking styles and the causal illusion. In Experiment 1, consistent with previous findings, we did not observe a significant association between the variables. However, a re-analysis revealed that participants displaying extreme response patterns (i.e., introducing the target cause in all trials) accounted for this result. Consequently, Experiment 2 addressed this issue by controlling the exposure to cause-present and cause-absent trials, eventually producing the expected pattern: the illusion was positively associated with intuitive thinking styles (Close-Minded Thinking, Preference for Intuitive Thinking) and negatively associated with a deliberate style (Actively Open-Minded Thinking).

data.title: A Peek into Token Bias: Large Language Models Are Not Yet Genuine Reasoners

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11050, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: This study introduces a hypothesis-testing framework to assess whether large language models (LLMs) possess genuine reasoning abilities or primarily depend on token bias. We go beyond evaluating LLMs on accuracy; rather, we aim to investigate their token bias in solving logical reasoning tasks. Specifically, we develop carefully controlled synthetic datasets, featuring conjunction fallacy and syllogistic problems. Our framework outlines a list of hypotheses where token biases are readily identifiable, with all null hypotheses assuming genuine reasoning capabilities of LLMs. The findings in this study suggest, with statistical guarantee, that most LLMs still struggle with logical reasoning. While they may perform well on classic problems, their success largely depends on recognizing superficial patterns with strong token bias, thereby raising concerns about their actual reasoning and generalization abilities.

data.title: How Cognitive Bias Shapes Gambling Behaviour and Consumer Vulnerability

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.64420/ijcp.v3i2.521?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.64420/ijcp.v3i2.521, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Background: The rapid expansion of digital gambling platforms significantly amplifies consumer vulnerability and gambling related harm, yet interdisciplinary literature synthe-sizing cognitive distortions, AI driven marketing personalization, and regulatory gover-nance gaps remains limited. Objective: This study aims to synthesize empirical and theo-retical evidence on how cognitive biases shape gambling behavior and consumer vulnera-bility across psychological, technological, socioeconomic, and regulatory dimensions. Methods: A qualitative literature review combining narrative and scoping review designs was conducted, examining 37 eligible studies selected via the PRISMA framework and ana-lyzed using thematic synthesis. Results: The findings demonstrate that cognitive biases, including the illusion of control, overconfidence bias, gambler's fallacy, and heuristic thin-king, interact with AI driven marketing personalization to reinforce persistent high-risk betting. These dynamics disproportionately harm vulnerable populations, culminating in acute psychological distress, severe debt accumulation, and broader socioeconomic insta-bility exacerbated by cross border regulatory deficits. Conclusion: Mitigating digital gam-bling harm requires an integrated framework combining ethical AI governance, transpa-rent marketing standards, public health interventions, and robust regulatory enforcement. Originality/Value: This review article advances scientific knowledge in the fields of beha-vioral economics, consumer psychology, and public health by synthesizing the evolving literature regarding cognitive biases and predictive digital marketing that has remained underexplored. It maps theoretical and methodological gaps while serving as a strategic reference for regulatory bodies and policymakers in formulating responsible gambling frameworks.
